nameStory: This tiny spider doesn't have a widely-used common name, so it goes by its scientific name Collinsia oxypaederotipus. The genus Collinsia was named after an early naturalist, while the species name 'oxypaederotipus' comes from Greek words meaning 'sharp-footed,' likely referring to some detail of its leg structure that early taxonomists found distinctive.
description: Collinsia oxypaederotipus is a dwarf spider, part of the sheet web weaver family that includes some of North America's tiniest spiders. Like other dwarf spiders, it's extremely small - likely only a few millimeters long - with the typical compact, rounded body shape of its family. These spiders are so small they're easily overlooked, living quiet lives among leaf litter and low vegetation. With only one recorded observation in New England, this species appears to be quite rare or easily missed in our region.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny, measuring just a few millimeters in body length - small enough to sit comfortably on your pinky fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with a relatively small cephalothorax (front section), giving it the typical 'dwarf spider' proportions

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates tiny sheet webs close to the ground - delicate, flat silk platforms that feel gossamer-thin and may collect morning dew

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves quickly when disturbed, scurrying through leaf litter with jerky, rapid movements typical of dwarf spiders

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight tiny dark eyes arranged in two rows on the front part of the body, though you'll need magnification to see the arrangement clearly

habitat: Found in ground-level microhabitats like leaf litter, moss, and low vegetation where humidity stays relatively high. Given its rarity in New England records, it likely prefers very specific conditions - possibly in undisturbed forest floors or specialized wetland edges. Look for it in areas with dense, decomposing organic matter that stays moist.

seasonality.spring: Adults may become active as temperatures warm, potentially emerging from winter hiding spots in leaf litter and beginning to establish small territories.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are likely mating and females are producing egg sacs, though the tiny webs are easily missed among summer vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Young spiders may be maturing to adult size, and adults might be preparing for winter by seeking protected overwintering sites in deep leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as adults or juveniles hidden deep in leaf litter, bark crevices, or other insulated microhabitats where they remain dormant.

funFact: This spider is so rarely observed that it's been recorded only once in all of New England, making any sighting a genuinely exciting discovery - you could be among the first people to document it in our region!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other dwarf spiders in the family Linyphiidae, which includes dozens of similarly tiny species. The only way to definitively identify this species is through microscopic examination of reproductive structures, so most field identifications must remain as 'dwarf spider species.'
contextualKnowledge: The scientific naming system becomes especially important with tiny spiders like this one, as common names are rarely established for species that are so small and uncommonly encountered. Many dwarf spiders lack common names entirely and are known primarily to specialists.
compareHints: Since this appears to be the only Collinsia species recorded in New England, compare it to other dwarf spiders in the Linyphiidae family. It shares the family's characteristic tiny size and sheet web construction, but specific identification requires expert examination. Most dwarf spiders look remarkably similar in the field, distinguished mainly by microscopic details of their reproductive anatomy.
